questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The long list of approved textbooks ______ on the notice board."
questions.explanation: The subject is *list*, which is singular, so the verb must be *is*. The phrase *of approved textbooks* only modifies the subject and cannot change its number. Cover any phrase beginning with *of* and the true subject becomes obvious.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with the nearest noun *textbooks* instead of the real subject *list*
distractorRationale.c: Same proximity error, and also shifts the sentence into the past
distractorRationale.d: Plural and perfect, so it doubles the error

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Neither the principal nor the teachers ______ present at the ceremony."
questions.explanation: With *either ... or* and *neither ... nor*, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The nearer subject here is the plural *teachers*, so the plural verb *were* is required. Reverse the order to "Neither the teachers nor the principal **was** present" and the verb changes with it.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with the further subject *principal* instead of the nearer one
distractorRationale.c: Singular and in the wrong tense for a completed past event
distractorRationale.d: Singular and present, so it fails on both number and tense

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Either the class captains or the head boy ______ to represent the school."
questions.explanation: Again the verb agrees with the nearer of the two subjects, and here the nearer one is the singular *head boy*, so *is going* is correct. This is the mirror image of the previous pattern, which shows that word order genuinely controls the choice.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with the further, plural subject *class captains*
distractorRationale.c: Plural and past, so it fails on both counts
distractorRationale.d: Plural and perfect, changing the meaning as well as the number

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Each of the candidates ______ been given a separate answer booklet."
questions.explanation: *Each*, *every*, *either*, *neither*, *one* and the -body and -one pronouns are all singular, so they take singular verbs. The subject is *Each*, not *candidates*, which sits inside the modifying phrase *of the candidates*.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with the plural noun *candidates* rather than with *Each*
distractorRationale.c: Plural, and *were been* is not a possible verb form
distractorRationale.d: Plural, and *are been* is likewise impossible

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Mathematics ______ the subject most candidates fear."
questions.explanation: Some nouns end in -s but are singular in meaning: mathematics, physics, economics, news, measles and mumps. They therefore take singular verbs, so *Mathematics is* is correct.

distractorRationale.a: Treats the final -s as a plural marker, which is the standard trap in this question type
distractorRationale.c: Plural and past, so it doubles the error
distractorRationale.d: Plural and perfect, changing both number and time reference

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The number of candidates registering for the examination ______ steadily each year."
questions.explanation: *The number of* is a singular expression — it names one figure — so it takes a singular verb. Contrast it with *a number of*, which means 'several' and takes a plural verb: "A number of candidates **are** waiting outside".

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with *candidates* instead of with the singular head *number*
distractorRationale.c: Plural, and the perfect aspect clashes with *each year*
distractorRationale.d: Plural and past, so the habitual present sense is lost too

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Twenty-five thousand naira ______ a reasonable price for that fabric."
questions.explanation: An amount of money, a distance, a period of time or a weight is treated as one single quantity, so it takes a singular verb. "Twenty years **is** a long time" and "Five kilometres **is** too far to walk" follow the same rule.

distractorRationale.a: Treats the sum as a collection of separate naira notes rather than as one price
distractorRationale.c: Plural and past, so both number and tense are wrong
distractorRationale.d: Plural and perfect, which also suggests the price has changed

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The jury ______ divided in their opinions about the evidence."
questions.explanation: A collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one body, but a plural verb when its members act individually. *Divided in their opinions* shows the members disagreeing among themselves, and the plural *their* confirms it, so the plural verb *are* is required.

distractorRationale.a: Would be correct in "The jury is considering the evidence", where the group acts as one unit, but it clashes with *their* here
distractorRationale.c: *Has divided* would mean the jury split something else into parts
distractorRationale.d: Singular and needlessly continuous, and still clashes with *their*

questions.stem: The sentence "The books on the top shelf is very dusty" is grammatically correct.
questions.explanation: False. The subject is the plural *books*, so the verb must be *are*. The singular *shelf* is only the object of the preposition *on* and has no influence on the verb. Cover the phrase *on the top shelf* and the correct agreement is immediately audible.

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "One of the boys who ______ selected for the quiz is my cousin."
questions.explanation: A relative pronoun takes its number from the noun it refers back to. *Who* here refers to *the boys*, because it is the boys who were selected, so the plural *were* is correct. The singular *is* later in the sentence belongs to the separate subject *One*, which is why both a plural and a singular verb appear in one sentence.

distractorRationale.a: Agrees with *One* rather than with the antecedent *boys*
distractorRationale.c: Singular and in the wrong tense for a completed selection
distractorRationale.d: Singular, and the perfect aspect does not fit a single past selection event
